title: GeoFidelity-Bench: Evaluating Block-Conditioned Geographic Fidelity in Text-to-Image Street-View Generation
claim: A benchmark pairs each target unit with real reference data, controlled prompt levels, generated outputs, and shared multi-metric evaluation.
layout: 3 columns, left-to-right; real and generated panels stacked, with arrows into evaluation
description: The figure has three columns, read left to right, with small arrows between them. The left card, 'Target block' (OSM named way), shows a map with a teal route and pin. Below it are a 'block key' box and a list of prompt levels L0, L1 and L2 in orange circles. The middle column has two stacked panels. The top teal 'Mapillary reference panel' lists a three-step chip pipeline (OSM match, fixed filters, panel selection) above stacked street photos of Paris, Tokyo and NYC. The bottom orange 'Generated panel' shows the L0, L1 and L2 prompt chips and the model count, above generated images of the same three cities. A 'same named block' pill links the two panels. The right blue 'Shared evaluation' column lists the vision encoders (DINOv2, Mask2Former) and four colored metric boxes: CosSim (marked main), DCSF/MMD, GAAS and Retrieval. A small 'Reports' box sits below. Teal marks real data and orange marks generated data. The eye goes first to the photo thumbnails and panel headers.
caption: Overview of GeoFidelity-Bench. Each target is a named OSM street block. Its geometry selects the Mapillary images that form the reference panel, and its metadata fills three prompt levels: city only (L0), street and neighborhood names (L1), and L1 plus GPS coordinates as text (L2). Six open-weight text-to-image models each generate four images per block and prompt level. Shared vision encoders compare the generated and reference panels through visual similarity, set fidelity and diversity, semantic attribute agreement, and retrieval against the panels of related blocks. Thumbnails show real references and SDXL images under L1 prompts for one block in each of Paris, Tokyo, and New York.
abstract: Text-to-image models can generate plausible street scenes from prompts such as "a street in New York City," but it remains unclear whether these images resemble the requested place or show a generic city appearance. Commonly used evaluation metrics mainly measure image quality or text alignment and do not directly assess geographic fidelity. We introduce GeoFidelity-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating whether generated street-view images match a target location at the level of named street blocks. The benchmark contains 112 street blocks from 25 cities across six continents, each paired with a panel of real Mapillary images and geographic metadata. From this metadata we build prompts with the city only, with street and neighborhood names, and with these names plus raw GPS coordinates. Across six open-weight text-to-image models, street and neighborhood names improve similarity to the target location, while raw GPS coordinates add only a small and uneven gain. Control prompts that swap in the names of other blocks while keeping the city fixed reduce retrieval accuracy, with larger decreases when the neighborhood name or both names are replaced. Generated images also distinguish their target blocks from local alternatives less reliably than held-out real images. CLIP alignment between generated images and their prompts is nearly uninformative about whether the images achieve block-level geographic fidelity. GeoFidelity-Bench provides a controlled testbed for studying location-conditioned generation and for measuring progress beyond generic city-level plausibility.
